page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Tool-call latency budget' and §4 'Multi-step reasoning cost'; propagates to §8 'Lesson' and 'Architectural actions'
quoted_clause: On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context; tool backends (search, SQL) add 50–150 ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead L_agent ≈ 220 ms (median).
observed: The 220 ms/turn orchestration figure is not reconcilable with the chapter's own per-turn model work, and the definition of L_agent is self-contradictory. The chapter calls L_agent 'the per-turn cost of the loop *around* the model' and then includes 'the LLM's short decision step to formulate the tool call', which is model inference, not overhead around it.
evidence: Under the chapter's own no-reuse policy, one agent turn costs: prefill of the grown prefix (10,065 tokens) = (10,065/9,200)×1.08 ≈ 1.18 s; decode of γ=65 tokens at 25 ms/token ≈ 1.63 s; tool ≈ 0.13 s → ≈2.94 s. The chapter's own W confirms this: W(3) − W(0) = 17.70 − 8.58 = 9.12 s over 3 turns ≈ 3.04 s/turn. A 120 ms 'agent step' is reachable only if the decision step's prefill is reduced to the ~865 newly appended tokens (≈100 ms), i.e. under prefix reuse — an assumption the L_agent paragraph never states, and one that contradicts the no-reuse framing in which β is presented. Consequently β(3)=1.08× and the §8 verdict ('added ~220 ms of orchestration latency', 'the trade-off was acceptable') understate the real per-turn cost by roughly an order of magnitude.
root_cause: Two accounting frames (orchestration-only vs. full per-turn model work) are merged under one symbol, and the 120 ms figure is imported without stating the cache policy that makes it attainable.
correction: Either (a) redefine L_agent as the tool-only leg (≈100–133 ms/turn) and rename β accordingly, or (b) state explicitly that the 120 ms decision step assumes prefix reuse of the grown prefix (≈865 new tokens ≈ 100 ms prefill) and that under the no-reuse policy the per-turn model work is ≈2.9 s. Then restate the §8 'Lesson' and 'Architectural actions' on the full per-turn cost, and reconcile with CH19-17 (the 100 ms vs 133 ms tool rate).
acceptance_test: A reader can compute the per-turn added latency under both cache policies from the chapter's own numbers and find that the 220 ms figure is either labelled tool-only or explicitly conditioned on prefix reuse; the §8 mini-case's headline conclusion cites the same per-turn figure the W table implies.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Event-level call ledger' (immediately above the ledger table)
quoted_clause: Boundary rule. A call's input never contains output tokens, so task_input must sum per-call inputs only — never the 'Total tokens (incl. 300 output)' column
observed: The stated rule is false as written and is contradicted by the ledger immediately below it. A call's input DOES contain prior turns' output tokens (the model's own γ reasoning and the tool-call text are part of the carried context).
evidence: The ledger's row 2 has 'Input before call 10,065' = 9,200 + 65 (call 1's γ output) + 800 (tool output) — i.e. call 2's input contains call 1's output tokens. The chapter itself states 'rows 1–3 are also the *next* call's input'. The rule is true only if restricted to a call's *own* output.
root_cause: A correct local rule ('do not add the final answer's 300 output tokens to a call's input') was over-generalized into an absolute.
correction: Restate: 'A call's input never contains its *own* output tokens; prior turns' outputs are part of the carried context. So task_input must sum per-call inputs only — never the "Total tokens (incl. 300 output)" column.'
acceptance_test: The rule as stated is compatible with every row of the event-level ledger without the reader having to notice an exception.

page_hint: Ch 19 §8 'Conditional completed-agent percentiles' vs. 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger'
quoted_clause: the *incremental* agent work beyond the single-shot baseline is zero, so it adds nothing to the p90/p95 values
observed: False for the unconditional distribution under the zero-turn convention, and contradicted ~200 words later in the same subsection by the chapter's own parenthetical.
evidence: Under the zero-turn convention the fallback contributes 0 ms of added orchestration, so it sorts to the *bottom* of the unconditional distribution: CDF(≤220 ms) = 2% + 68% = 70%; CDF(≤440 ms) = 95.0%; CDF(≤660 ms) = 100%. The unconditional p95 therefore reads 440 ms, not 660 ms. The chapter states this itself: 'under the zero-turn convention it lands exactly on the boundary, CDF(T ≤ 2) = 95.0%, and reads T = 2 → 440 ms'. The p90 is unchanged (440 ms) but the p95 changes from 660 ms to 440 ms.
root_cause: The conditional (renormalized, fallback excluded) and unconditional (fallback zero-weighted) conventions are described in the same breath; the fallback 'adds nothing' only because it is excluded, not because it contributes zero.
correction: State all three conventions explicitly: (i) conditional on completed runs (98% renormalized): p50/p90/p95 = 220/440/660 ms; (ii) unconditional with the fallback zero-weighted: p95 = 440 ms (the 2% mass sorts to the bottom); (iii) unconditional with the fallback at its true 860 ms: p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms.
acceptance_test: All three conventions' p50/p90/p95/p99 can be reproduced from the stated distribution, and no sentence asserts that the fallback cannot move a percentile under a convention where it does.

quoted_clause: At the canonical workload's ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (L_exec = λ × W_exec ≈ 10 × 8.6 per Ch 4; distinct from the ~100 *active-user* population) with the median single-turn profile (~27.2 GB/request at 10,365 tokens), the aggregate KV alone is ~86 × 27.2 GB ≈ 2.3 TB — far beyond one host's ~436 GB KV budget, so agents do not just stress memory, they force a fleet (Chapter 17).
observed: The fleet argument is framed against a single host rather than against the canonical deployment's actual fleet, and it mixes two conventions: single-shot concurrency with agentic per-request KV, understating the agentic aggregate.
evidence: 86 in-flight comes from the single-shot service time (10 × 8.6). The agentic service time is 11.52 s at the median T=1 and 17.70 s at T=3, so in-flight = 10 × 11.52 ≈ 115 and 10 × 17.70 = 177. Aggregate KV: single-shot 86 × 24.9 = 2,141 GB; agentic median 115 × 27.2 ≈ 3,133 GB (1.46×); agentic p95 177 × 31.7 ≈ 5,611 GB (2.62×). Comparing 2.3 TB with one host's 436 GB is a weak claim for a deployment the book elsewhere describes as a multi-host fleet.
root_cause: Ch 4's single-shot concurrency figure was reused without recomputing it for the agentic service time, and the rhetorical target ('one host') is not the decision-relevant comparison.
correction: Recompute in-flight from the agentic W and state the marginal fleet growth: aggregate KV demand is ≈1.46× (median) to ≈2.62× (p95) the single-shot baseline, then convert to a marginal host delta using Ch 17's canonical fleet size and peak rate. Cross-reference the Ch 17 host count explicitly.
acceptance_test: The in-flight figure used in the KV aggregate is derived from the same service time used in the same paragraph, and the paragraph states a marginal host delta rather than a single-host comparison.

quoted_clause: a 10% cheaper pipeline that fails 5% more often can be net more expensive once retries and human intervention are counted
observed: Under the relative reading the arithmetic is backwards; only the percentage-point reading supports the claim, and the text does not say which reading it means.
evidence: Relative reading: cost per successful task ∝ 0.90/0.95 = 0.947, i.e. 5.3% *cheaper*, not more expensive. Percentage-point reading (e.g. success 90% → 85%): 0.90/0.85 = 1.059, i.e. 5.9% more expensive — the claim holds. The chapter elsewhere insists on explicit denominators and operating points, so the ambiguity is out of character.
root_cause: Relative vs. absolute percentage ambiguity in a chapter that otherwise guards against exactly this class of error.
correction: Write the example with explicit numbers: 'a pipeline 10% cheaper per attempt whose success rate falls from 90% to 85% raises cost per successful task by 0.90/0.85 ≈ 1.06× before counting retries and human intervention.'
acceptance_test: The example's arithmetic is reproducible from the stated numbers under the reading the text adopts, and the reading is stated.

quoted_clause: this chapter uses the narrower abbreviation RQA only where the retrieval-augmented search/answer step is meant specifically (the retrieval leg + single generation) ... The two are not used interchangeably; Table 19-1 and the glossary follow this same rule.
observed: The chapter's own usage contradicts the definition it establishes, and the chapter promises a discipline it does not follow.
evidence: RQA is used throughout for multi-turn agentic pipelines: §2 'a complex RQA request ... may traverse three or more cycles'; §3 'Take a user query routed to an agentic RQA pipeline'; §8 'An enterprise RQA system serves 2,000 knowledge workers' with a 3-turn agentic layer; Table 19-1's title 'Token amplification and latency trade-offs for agentic RQA pipelines'. None of these is 'the retrieval leg + single generation'.
root_cause: The terminology note was written for a narrower scope than the chapter's actual subject.
correction: Either narrow the definition to 'retrieval-augmented question answering, agentic or single-shot' and drop the 'retrieval leg + single generation' qualifier, or reserve RQA for the single-generation retrieval leg and use 'agentic RAG' for the multi-turn pipelines. Then reconcile Table 19-1's title and the glossary entry.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of RQA in Ch 19 and in the glossary is consistent with the definition in §1.

page_hint: Ch 19 §2 'Mental Model' (final paragraph) vs. §4 'Measurement' scoping note
quoted_clause: The critical insight for capacity planning is that each cycle incurs a fixed overhead: one LLM inference turn plus any tool-call latency.

quoted_clause: Architectural actions. The team sets the turn limit to 3, instruments each turn's token and orchestration latency, and adds a context cache for the search tool.
observed: The mini-case's actions and its verdict omit the lever that dominates the economics, and the 'acceptable' verdict rests on the smallest of the three cost terms.
evidence: The chapter's own numbers: processed tokens per submitted request = 23,927 vs 9,500 baseline = 2.52×; full service time 17.70 s vs 8.58 s = 2.06×; billed tokens under no-reuse 4.47× vs under 100% prefix reuse 12,290/9,500 ≈ 1.29×. The search-tool cache the team adds yields, by the chapter's own note, 'no LLM-token or KV-resident saving'. The dominant lever (prefix caching / compaction, named in §6) is never adopted or priced in the mini-case, and 'The trade-off was acceptable' is justified only by the ~220 ms orchestration overhead.
root_cause: The mini-case's decision narrative was built around the latency metric rather than the cost metric the chapter itself identifies as the agentic unit of value.
correction: Add prefix caching (or compaction) as an explicit action with its measured effect (billed 4.47× → ≈1.29×; W 17.70 s → 14.16 s; KV residency unchanged), and restate the verdict against cost per successful task rather than orchestration overhead.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's 'Lesson' quantifies the cost effect of the actions it recommends, and the verdict is stated in the same units as §6's cost-per-successful-task objective.

quoted_clause: Inference scaling. The base model (70B FP16, 8×H100) must now serve variable-length contexts, and — critically — the KV-residency conclusion is far more severe than a per-latency convenience
observed: The chapter computes the prefill/decode mix shift but never interprets it. This is the most consequential systems consequence of the agentic layer and the one that connects to the book's prefill/decode, chunked-prefill and scheduling chapters.
evidence: From the chapter's own W: single-shot prefill share = 1.08/8.58 = 12.6% and prefill/decode ratio = 1.08/7.5 = 0.14; at T=3 no-reuse, prefill share = 4.93/17.70 = 27.8% and prefill/decode ratio = 4.93/12.375 = 0.40. The number of prefills per request goes from 1 to T+1 = 4. The chapter computes all of these numbers but never interprets them as a regime change (arithmetic intensity, KV pressure per unit of decode, prefill/decode interference in the scheduler, chunked-prefill policy).
root_cause: The chapter treats agentic depth as a token/KV-count story and stops before the regime consequence, breaking the book's causal chain from request shape to scheduler behaviour.
correction: Add a short subsection stating: agentic workloads are structurally more prefill-heavy; the prefill/decode ratio rises from ≈0.14 to ≈0.40 at T=3; therefore chunked prefill, prefix caching and prefill/decode scheduling policies that were optional for single-shot traffic become first-order for agentic traffic. Cross-reference the relevant chapters.
acceptance_test: A reader can state, from this chapter alone, how the prefill/decode balance of an agentic workload differs from single-shot and name one scheduling or serving consequence.

page_hint: Ch 19 §6 'Three policies, three different levers'; Fig 19.3 caption
quoted_clause: Prefix-cache eviction moves neither: the request still carries the full accumulated context (34.0 GB at turn 4), so its own KV is unchanged — what changes is the reusable cached prefix, which is freed and must be re-prefilled on the next turn.
observed: The three bars of Fig 19.3 are not on a common baseline, and the third is not a state-management policy for the request's own context.
evidence: The append-only bar is defined by §6's policy (iv) 'no prefix cache is assumed to be reused across turns' — i.e. there is no prefix cache in that scenario. 'Prefix-cache eviction' presupposes a populated prefix cache, so it describes a policy for a different baseline (a system that does use prefix caching). It also does not affect whether the request's own context grows unbounded, which is the criterion §6 sets for a state-management policy ('that policy — not the model — determines whether context grows unbounded').
root_cause: A cache-capacity policy was placed in a figure titled 'State-management policy', and the per-bar baseline is not stated.
correction: Either (a) replace the third bar with 'prefix-cache reuse' (which reduces billable tokens but not KV residency — the distinction §6 draws) so all three bars share the append-only baseline, or (b) keep eviction but label each bar with its baseline (no-cache / no-cache / with-cache) and retitle the figure 'Three levers move three different quantities'.
acceptance_test: Each bar of Fig 19.3 states its baseline policy, and the figure's title matches the set of policies shown.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Token-quantity definitions' table and the two 'Billed, ...' bullets
quoted_clause: cached / uncached / billed | fraction of task_input served by prefix cache vs re-processed; billed per provider rules | a cache hit makes billed input smaller than task_input
observed: 'Billed' is used in two incompatible senses — provider-charged tokens (per the table's own definition) and tokens processed/re-computed (per the bullets).
evidence: The bullets then read 'Billed, no prefix cache: 41,990 input + 495 output = 42,485 tokens' and 'Billed, perfect prefix cache: ... 12,290 tokens'. Under a provider that charges a discounted but non-zero rate for cached tokens, the billed total under perfect prefix reuse is not 12,290; 12,290 is the processed (FLOP-bearing) total. The chapter's own §4 text compounds this: 'billed/FLOP input differs from context-carried input' merges two of the three quantities.

acceptance_test: Every occurrence of 'billed' in Ch 19 refers to one quantity, and the two processed totals are labelled as processed.

quoted_clause: Turn 2: Input: 10,350 tokens; Model decides to synthesize: emits a final answer
observed: §3's turn numbering collides with §4's definition of T, so the same label means different things within one chapter.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Billed, perfect prefix cache' bullet and the W_reuse(3) computation
quoted_clause: Billed, perfect prefix cache: only each call's newly appended tokens are re-processed, 9,200 + 3 × 865 = 11,795 input + 495 output = 12,290 tokens.
observed: The reuse prefill double-counts the γ tokens, and the attribution ('each call's newly appended tokens') is wrong for the synthesis call.
evidence: Under strict prefix reuse, the tokens newly *prefilled* per call are: call 2 → 800 (tool output only; γ₁ was decoded by call 1 and its KV is already resident), call 3 → 800, call 4 → 800. Total prefill = 9,200 + 3×800 = 11,600, not 11,795. The synthesis call adds 0 new tokens (its input equals call 3's post-call context). The 195-token difference moves W_reuse(3) by ≈0.02 s (14.16 → 14.14 s), so the printed numbers are essentially unaffected, but the accounting rule is stated incorrectly.
root_cause: 'Newly appended' was equated with 'newly prefilled'; decoded tokens are appended but already resident in the KV cache.
correction: State the reuse prefill as 9,200 + 3×800 = 11,600 (γ tokens are already resident from decode) and note that the synthesis call adds no new prefill; recompute the W_reuse column from it.
acceptance_test: The reuse prefill total equals the number of tokens never previously prefilled, and the printed W_reuse values are recomputed from it.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Multi-step reasoning cost' (W computation) and Table 19-1 caption
quoted_clause: yields a prefill sum of (41,990 / 9,200) × 1.08 ≈ 4.93 s
observed: Prefill time is scaled linearly in tokens, ignoring the quadratic attention term, and the approximation is presented without qualification.
evidence: For the canonical geometry implied by the 2.62 MB/token KV figure (80 layers, d_model 8,192), attention is ≈17% of prefill FLOPs at 9,200 tokens and ≈22% at 11,795. The magnitude is small at these lengths, but the linear form is used for every W column.

correction: Either state the linear approximation explicitly as a bound ('prefill time is taken linear in tokens; the quadratic attention term adds ≈2% at these lengths') or use FLOP-ratio scaling. Verify against Ch 8's prefill model before changing numbers.
acceptance_test: The chapter states whether prefill time is linear in tokens and, if so, the error bound at the canonical lengths.

quoted_clause: §3.1: "the number of distinct prompt-pattern classes an adversary can successfully submit through all user-facing entry points" | §4.1: "**PIES** | DERIVED | Unique, non-redundant prompt-injection patterns across all entry points" | §8: "PIES has dropped from 217 to 143 after adding a prompt-scanning guardrail"
observed: The chapter carries two incompatible definitions of its central metric. §3.1 defines PIES as the classes an adversary can *successfully* submit (a success-conditioned count); §4.1 defines it as *unique patterns* (a pattern-space count). The worked arithmetic in §3.1 implements only the pattern-space reading — 4 x 8 x 6 x 4 = 768 candidates, deduplicated to 217, with no success criterion applied anywhere. The mini-case then reports a PIES *drop* (217 -> 143 -> 138) caused by adding a guardrail, which is only meaningful under the success reading; under the §4.1 pattern-space reading a guardrail cannot change the pattern space at all, so the headline trajectory of the chapter's capstone is unexplained by the metric as defined in the metric table.
evidence: §3.1 arithmetic: 4 entry points x 8 delimiters x 6 templates x 4 context segments = 768; 'After deduplication by normalized edit distance at a fixed threshold ... the unique exposure surface is PIES = 217' — no success filter. §4.1 metric row omits 'successfully'. §6 consequence 1: 'reducing PIES by roughly a third - ~34% (the §8 mini-case's worked instance: 217 -> 143)' — a guardrail changing a pattern count. §5 mistake table: 'Deduplicate by normalized syntax and report PIES' — again the pattern-space reading.
root_cause: The metric was defined with a success qualifier, then computed as a pure pattern-space count; the two readings were never reconciled, and the mini-case silently adopted the third (guardrail-reduced) reading.
correction: Choose one definition and make every occurrence match. Recommended: keep the §3.1 arithmetic but rename it (e.g. 'candidate pattern space CPS = 217'), and define PIES as the subset of candidate classes that produced at least one guardrail bypass in the cycle; then the mini-case's 217 -> 143 -> 138 becomes 'successful classes', and Table 24-1's PIES row must be re-derived under that definition. Alternative: keep PIES as the pattern-space count, hold it constant across cycles, and move the guardrail effect entirely onto the red-team win rate and guardrail-trigger rate rows (which already carry it), rewriting §6 consequence 1 and §8 accordingly. Update §4.1's definition and the §5 mistake row to match whichever is chosen.
acceptance_test: §3.1, §4.1, §6, §8 and Table 24-1 use one definition; every PIES value in the chapter is reproducible from the stated rule under that definition; the mini-case's PIES trajectory is explained by the mechanism named in the prose; the §5 mistake row and the §4.1 metric row describe the same quantity.

page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3 ('The Architecture That Fails'), checks 1-3 and the Outcome paragraph
quoted_clause: "Dividing peak demand by theoretical peak gives **6.5 hosts - and that is a *theoretical compute floor*, not a production sizing result.**" | "**Outcome.** The Red Team's adversarial pass (checks 1-3) rejects Candidate A and leaves Candidate B as a candidate *pending measurement*."
observed: The Red Team's three checks cover peak prefill compute, failure domain, and utilization, but never the KV-residency screen at peak - which the rest of this book identifies as the binding screen for this workload. The chapter computes the KV screen only at average load ('~5 hosts at 10 rps'). At the canonical peak the KV screen is ~19.6 hosts (21 with N-1), so Candidate B (8 hosts) is roughly 2.5x short of the canonical screen and would be rejected by the same screen that rejects Candidate A. The Outcome paragraph therefore reports a survivor that the book's own Ch 17/20/25 arithmetic eliminates, and the case's host counts (4 vs 8) are irreconcilable with the canonical fleet (21 KV / 19-22 prefill / 32-34 with the 70% x 95% + N-1 policy).
evidence: Recomputation at peak: 40 rps x 8.6 s = 344 in-flight requests; 344 x 24.9 GB = 8,565.6 GB; 8,565.6 / 436 GB per host = 19.65 hosts (+N-1 = 21). Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1: 'KV-residency screen (Ch 17 Table 17-1): 21 hosts (KV, case-independent)'. Ch 25 §8: 'the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen'. Ch 24 §3.3 itself: 'The KV-residency screen independently needs ~5 hosts at 10 rps on the FP16-KV basis'.
root_cause: The case was sized from the prefill screen alone; the screen the book elsewhere identifies as binding was never applied at the operating point under test, and the case's scale was never reconciled with the canonical fleet.
correction: Add a fourth Red Team check (peak KV residency) and reconcile the outcome. Either (a) re-scale the candidate pair so the case is consistent with the canonical screens (e.g. A = 12 hosts, B = 24 hosts, with the KV screen computed for each), or (b) declare the case a scaled-down illustration with an explicit scale factor and state which conclusions transfer and which do not. In either case the Outcome paragraph must state which candidates survive the full screen set, not only the prefill screen.
acceptance_test: The §3.3 candidate host counts are reconciled with Ch 17 Table 17-1 and Ch 25 ADR 0015 R1 (21 KV / 19-22 prefill / 32-34 with policy); the KV screen is computed at peak as well as average; the Outcome paragraph names the screen that eliminates each candidate.

quoted_clause: "a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer (an arrival-rate buffer: outage bursts queue for drain rather than being served live - 200 rps x ~7 TFLOP ~= 1.4 PFLOPS exceeds one H100's ~0.989 PFLOPS peak)"
observed: The mini-case's own arithmetic shows that one H100 cannot serve the burst even at 100% of theoretical peak, let alone at a realistic efficiency; the 'buffer' defers the burst rather than absorbing it, so the queued requests cannot meet the stated 3 s SLO. The burst duration is never given, so neither the queue depth nor the drain time can be computed. The chapter nevertheless closes with 'The customer's vague excitement became a defensible, bounded, shippable scope', presenting a single-GPU recommendation whose own arithmetic contradicts the SLO it claims to meet.
evidence: 200 rps x (2 x 7e9 params x 500 tokens) = 200 x 7e12 FLOP/s = 1.4e15 FLOP/s = 1.4 PFLOPS vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak (the chapter's own figures). At the 30-40% sustained MFU used elsewhere in the book, one H100 delivers ~0.30-0.40 PFLOPS, so the burst alone needs ~3.5-4.7 GPUs. No burst duration is stated anywhere in the mini-case.
root_cause: Queueing is treated as a capacity solution rather than as a transfer of the problem into latency, and the missing burst duration makes the queue uncomputable, so the SLO consequence is never faced.
correction: State the burst duration and rate; compute the queue depth (arrival rate x duration) and the drain time at the sustainable rate; then state explicitly that burst-window requests miss the 3 s SLO and choose one of: (a) a separate burst SLO or degraded mode, (b) size for the burst (>= 4 H100s for prefill alone), or (c) a named fallback path. Restate the closing sentence so it does not claim the 3 s SLO is met during the burst.
acceptance_test: The mini-case states burst duration, queue depth, drain time, and the SLO outcome for burst-window requests; the recommended GPU count is consistent with the burst arithmetic printed in the same paragraph.

quoted_clause: "**Red-team win rate** | DERIVED | Proportion of evaluation cycles where Red Team escapes all guardrails | -> 0 over time" | Table 24-1: "Red-team win rate | 8% | 3.5% | 1.2%"
observed: The metric's denominator (cycles) is incompatible with the tabulated values. Over three cycles, a proportion of cycles can only be 0%, 33.3%, 66.7%, or 100%. The tabulated 8% / 3.5% / 1.2% are per-probe escape rates. The mini-case repeats the per-probe reading ('the Red-team win rate dropping from 8% to 1.2% over three simulated cycles'), so the definition in §4.1 is the outlier.
evidence: Table 24-1 columns are Cycle 1 / Cycle 2 / Cycle 3; §4.2 item 1: 'runs 1,000 Red Team probes per cycle'; §8: 'the Red-team win rate dropping from 8% to 1.2% over three simulated cycles'.
root_cause: The denominator was changed from probes to cycles in the metric definition without updating the definition or the data, and the false-positive row's explicit denominator note ('denominator = interventions, not queries') shows the convention was applied there but not here.
correction: Define red-team win rate as 'fraction of Red Team probes in a cycle that achieve an unintended outcome (denominator = probes, not cycles)' and keep the table values; or keep the per-cycle definition and re-tabulate as counts of escaping cycles. State the denominator explicitly in the metric table, as the false-positive row does.
acceptance_test: The definition's denominator matches the tabulated values and the mini-case prose; a reader can recompute 8% from 1,000 probes (80 escapes) and the table's Cycle 3 value from the Cycle 3 probe count.

quoted_clause: "**Candidate A: 4xH100 hosts**, 8-bit KV, tight batching target (batch <= 8), minimal headroom." | "**Candidate B: 8xH100 hosts**, FP16 KV, batching target set by the analysis rather than pre-declared."
observed: Three variables differ simultaneously between the two candidates - host count (4 vs 8), KV precision (8-bit vs FP16), and batching target (batch <= 8 vs analysis-derived). The chapter's own text shows the KV screen differs between them (4.9 hosts on the FP16 basis vs ~2.5 on the 8-bit basis), so the '45% per-token cost' delta and the Red Team's rejection cannot be attributed to host count, to KV precision, or to batching. The Outcome paragraph nonetheless attributes the result to sizing ('sized to the average, not to the peaks, the tail, or the failure domain'), which the design does not isolate.
evidence: §3.3: 'Candidate A's 8-bit KV halves its own KV screen to ~2.5 hosts'; 'the two screens converge near 5 hosts: prefill binds outright for Candidate A's 8-bit KV (KV screen ~2.5), and on the FP16 basis the binding screen flips near ~33% sustained MFU'.
root_cause: The case was written as a narrative with two named bundles rather than as a controlled comparison in which one variable moves at a time.
correction: Either hold KV precision and batching target constant across the pair (A = 4 hosts FP16, B = 8 hosts FP16) and treat KV precision as a separate lever discussed afterwards, or state explicitly that the pair is a bundle and that every conclusion is about the bundle, not about host count. In the latter case the Outcome paragraph must say so.
acceptance_test: The §3.3 text names the variable each conclusion depends on; the cost delta is attributed to a single variable or explicitly to the bundle; no conclusion is drawn about host count alone.

page_hint: Ch 24 §4.2 (item 3) vs §4.1 metric table, §8 mini-case, Table 24-1
quoted_clause: "**Retrieval auditor** - samples 100 retrievals per cycle and manually verifies whether any returned chunk is poisoned." | Table 24-1: "Poisoned-hit rate | 0.006 | 0.003 | 0.0025"

page_hint: Ch 22, Note 22.1-1 (the paragraph beginning 'Scope the rate comparison')
quoted_clause: "~1.19 PFLOPS is the **aggregate (whole-model) linear-only deadline demand** for one 9.2K prefill, so it may be compared only against an equally-scoped **aggregate host peak - 8 x 0.989 = 7.91 PFLOPS** - which it clears with headroom"

At the canonical 10 rps average, prefill demand is 10 x 1.288 = 12.9 PFLOP/s, which exceeds a whole host's 7.91 PFLOPS peak. As written, 'clears with headroom' invites the inference that one 8xH100 host serves the canonical workload - a conclusion the same book contradicts in Ch 24 §3.3 (1.6 hosts at 100% of peak, ~4.1 at 40% MFU, at 10 rps alone).
evidence: 10 x 1.288 PFLOP = 12.88 PFLOP/s vs 8 x 0.989 = 7.91 PFLOPS. Ch 24 §3.3: 'it only needs ~1.6 nodes of prefill compute *at the idealized 100% theoretical efficiency*' and 'at the 30-40% sustained MFU ... that 1.6-node floor becomes ~4-5 nodes'.
root_cause: The note scopes the comparison to one request but omits the load-aggregate comparison the book makes elsewhere, leaving the reader to generalize a per-request headroom statement to a per-load one.
correction: Add the aggregate comparison explicitly: 'one 9.2K prefill clears a host's peak, but the canonical 10 rps average is 12.9 PFLOP/s of prefill demand - 1.6 hosts at 100% of peak and ~4.1 at 40% MFU (Ch 24 §3.3) - so the headroom statement is per-request, not per-load.'

quoted_clause: "**Decision:** Render the KV cache in FP8 for the long-context decode path, keeping prefill and the retrieval/prompt phase in FP16."
observed: As written the decision describes two KV precisions for one sequence. The KV cache is produced by the prefill forward pass and consumed by every decode step; a configuration that keeps prefill in FP16 and decode in FP8 is not implementable without a conversion step, and the conversion would cost the very memory saving the decision is meant to deliver. The decision is phrased by pipeline phase rather than by artifact.
evidence: KV tensors are written during prefill and read during decode; the chapter's own §8 evidence line treats the KV cache as a single resident artifact ('a 9,500-token FP8 KV ~= 12.45 GB/request').
root_cause: The decision was drafted by naming the pipeline stages involved rather than the artifact whose precision is being chosen.
correction: Restate as: 'Compute prefill in FP16 and quantize the K/V tensors to FP8 on write, so the resident KV cache is FP8 for both the prefill output and every decode read; the retrieval/prompt phase remains FP16.' If the intent is a phase-dependent policy (FP16 KV for short contexts, FP8 for long), state the switch rule and the threshold.
acceptance_test: The Decision names the artifact (the resident KV cache), the write path, and the read path; no reader can infer two KV precisions for one sequence.

page_hint: Ch 25 §8 (ADR 0017, Alternatives considered #1 and Consequences) vs §6 (ADR 0015, requirement matrix R1)
quoted_clause: "1. *Add capacity* - rejected as the first move: the canonical peak already needs 21 hosts on the KV screen (22 under the case (ii) prefill screen; Ch 16/17/20)" | ADR 0015 R1: "KV-residency screen (Ch 17 Table 17-1): 21 hosts (KV, case-independent)"
observed: ADR 0017's decision halves KV residency, which halves the very screen it cites: the peak KV screen moves from 21 hosts to roughly 11 (344 in-flight / 35.0 concurrent per host = 9.8, +N-1 = 11). The ADR's Consequences section never states the revised fleet count, and ADR 0015's requirement matrix still carries '21 hosts (KV, case-independent)' as the operative screen. Once ADR 0017 is adopted, the two records in the same chapter cannot both be current.
evidence: 436 GB / 12.45 GB = 35.0 concurrent per host (vs 17.5 at FP16); 344 / 35.0 = 9.8 hosts, +1 for N-1 = 11. ADR 0017's own numbers: 'the same ~436 GB budget holds ~35.0 concurrent 9,500-token requests instead of ~17.5'.
root_cause: The ADR was written as a single-host memory decision and never propagated to the fleet-level screen it invalidates.
correction: Add a fleet-level consequence to ADR 0017 ('the peak KV-residency screen moves from 21 hosts to ~11; ADR 0015 R1 must be re-screened on adoption') and add an explicit review trigger in ADR 0017 pointing at ADR 0015's R1 row.
acceptance_test: ADR 0017 states the post-decision host count; ADR 0015 R1 carries a review trigger naming ADR 0017; the two records cannot both be current without a note saying which supersedes which.

page_hint: Ch 25 §8 (ADR 0017, Alternatives considered #1) vs Ch 22 §6 and Ch 25 §6 (ADR 0015 Context)
quoted_clause: "relieving the memory ceiling by adding hosts multiplies the fleet cost (each 8xH100 is ~$5.8K/mo amortized)" | ADR 0015: "~$155.8K/mo (~$24.97/1K) self-host"
observed: The two per-host cost bases in the same chapter do not reconcile. 21 hosts x $5.8K/mo = $121.8K/mo, but the canonical self-host figure used twice in this chapter is ~$155.8K/mo - a $34.0K/mo (28%) gap that is not itemized anywhere in the chunk. If $5.8K is hardware-only amortization, the ADR understates the marginal cost of 'add capacity' by about 22% ($7.42K/host implied by $155.8K / 21), which materially weakens the rejection of alternative #1 - the very alternative the decision is chosen over.
root_cause: Two different per-host cost bases are in circulation (hardware-only amortization vs all-in) and the ADR uses the lower one without stating what it includes.
correction: State what $5.8K/mo covers and reconcile with Ch 16's build-up. If it is hardware-only, write '~$5.8K/mo hardware amortization (~$7.4K/mo all-in including power, ops and colo, Ch 16)' and use the all-in figure in the rejection of 'add capacity'.
acceptance_test: Multiplying the stated per-host cost by the canonical host count reproduces the canonical monthly figure, or the difference is explicitly itemized in the same paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 23 §8 (mini-case, dialogue summary and mirrored restatement)
quoted_clause: "quality means 'resolve the ticket, not just answer' (a capability that rules out the cheaper model)" | "a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, ... quality-gated on real resolved tickets"
observed: The dialogue establishes a capability requirement that is said to rule out the cheaper model, and the scope then selects a 7B-class model without stating how the capability is met or which model was ruled out. The capability requirement also disappears from the mirrored restatement, which carries instead a process gate ('quality-gated on real resolved tickets') - a different kind of bound. A bound introduced in the dialogue is therefore dropped between the dialogue and the restatement, which is precisely the failure mode the chapter's own §4 metric ('Customer buy-in - did the mirrored restatement get an explicit yes?') is meant to catch.
evidence: The mini-case's own text: the capability constraint appears once, in the traffic/quality enumeration; the final scope contains no capability requirement.
root_cause: The dialogue's capability constraint and the scope's model choice were written independently and never reconciled.
correction: Name the tier that was ruled out and why (e.g. 'a 7B model cannot resolve tickets end-to-end; the draft-and-verify path is out of scope for this release'), and carry the capability requirement into the mirrored restatement as a bound with its own acceptance test.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's final scope contains a capability requirement and a model choice consistent with the dialogue's constraint; every bound introduced in the dialogue appears in the restatement.

observed: The bare three-backtick run opens an inline code span that never closes - there is no other three-backtick run in the paragraph - so a CommonMark/Pandoc renderer treats the remainder of the list item (', `{{`, `[[`, `[INST]`)') as literal code text, rendering the tail of the list in monospace with visible backticks. The example delimiter is itself a Markdown delimiter and was placed inside a code span without escaping.
evidence: Code-span matching requires the closing backtick run to have the same length as the opener; the surrounding runs are all length 1, so the length-3 opener is never closed.
root_cause: An example string that is itself a Markdown delimiter was inserted into a code span without escaping.
correction: Escape the backticks inside the code span, or replace the example with a delimiter that is not a Markdown delimiter (e.g. `<|im_start|>`, `<s>`, `###`).
acceptance_test: The rendered page shows the eight delimiters as one inline code span, with no literal backticks and no monospace run extending past the end of the list item.

quoted_clause: "under the canonical assumptions the prefill-compute and KV-capacity terms are where the pressure lands, not decode bandwidth."
observed: The exclusionary phrasing invites the reader to conclude that decode bandwidth is not a constraint, while §6 of the same chapter shows decode requires 5.6 TB/s sustained - above a single GPU's 3.35 TB/s - so decode bandwidth is a binding per-host constraint that tensor parallelism relieves. The benign reading (fleet-scaling pressure vs per-host constraint) is available but is never stated.
evidence: §6: 'requires a weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step ... each GPU streams only ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35 TB/s'.
root_cause: 'Pressure' is used in Step 4 to mean fleet-scaling pressure and in §6 to mean per-host constraint, with no disambiguation.
correction: Qualify: 'the pressure that scales the fleet lands on prefill compute and KV capacity; decode bandwidth is a per-host constraint that tensor parallelism relieves rather than one that adds hosts.'
acceptance_test: Step 4's sentence and §6's arithmetic cannot be read as contradictory by a reader who has read both.

quoted_clause: "The 30x input/output ratio means this workload's prefill phase dominates: ~1.29 PFLOP of compute per request"
observed: 'Dominates' is unqualified. Prefill dominates the FLOP budget (1.29 PFLOP against ~42 TFLOP of decode) but not the latency budget: 300 output tokens at ~25 ms is ~7.5 s of decode against ~1.08 s of prefill inside the canonical 8.6 s service time. A reader can carry away the opposite of the truth about where the request's time goes.
evidence: 300 x 25 ms = 7.5 s; 8.6 s service time - 7.5 s decode ~= 1.1 s, consistent with the 1.08 s prefill budget used in Note 22.1-1.
root_cause: 'Dominates' is used without naming the dimension it dominates.
correction: Write 'the prefill phase dominates the compute budget (not the latency budget: decode contributes ~7.5 s of the canonical 8.6 s service time)'.
acceptance_test: The sentence names the dimension it dominates, and the reader can reconcile it with the 8.6 s service time.

quoted_clause: "~1.19 PFLOPS required at the ~1.08 s budget"
observed: The 1.08 s prefill budget is used twice without derivation or a cross-reference, so the reader cannot tell where it comes from or how it relates to the canonical TTFT <= 2 s (p95) or the 8.6 s service time. The number is recoverable by subtraction (8.6 s service time minus ~7.5 s of decode), which suggests it is imported from Ch 8's latency decomposition - but the pointer is missing.
root_cause: The budget was imported from another chapter without a pointer, so the chapter's most load-bearing constant is unverifiable in place.
correction: Add the pointer and the derivation, e.g. 'the ~1.08 s prefill budget (Ch 8's canonical TTFT decomposition: 8.6 s service time minus ~7.5 s of decode)'.
acceptance_test: The 1.08 s figure is traceable to a named section and its relation to the 2 s TTFT SLO is stated.

page_hint: Ch 22 §7 (What We Still Don't Know, bullets 1 and 4)
quoted_clause: "the 3.35 TB/s H100 figure is a theoretical peak and real serving kernels may sustain less. (a hypothesis awaiting verification)" | "HBM3e and MI300X publish higher peaks, which would move the GPU-count equation without changing the compute-bound vs bandwidth-bound classification. (a hypothesis awaiting verification)"
observed: In both bullets the parenthetical label attaches to the whole bullet, but the leading clause is a first-party specification (a FACT) and the second bullet's conclusion is an analytical derivation, not a hypothesis. Only 'real serving kernels may sustain less' is a hypothesis. The house convention binds a label to its clause, so these are wrong-span applications.
evidence: 3.35 TB/s is the H100's published HBM3 peak; HBM3e and MI300X peaks are published specifications; 'would move the GPU-count equation without changing the regime classification' follows from the roofline argument already given in the chapter.
root_cause: Labels were placed at bullet level rather than at clause level.
correction: Split the labels: '[1P][FACT] - 3.35 TB/s is the H100's theoretical HBM peak; [HYPOTHESIS] - real serving kernels sustain less.' and '[1P][FACT] - HBM3e and MI300X publish higher peaks; [DERIVED] - that moves the GPU-count equation without changing the regime classification.'
acceptance_test: Every clause in §7 carries a label matching its epistemic status, and no FACT clause is covered by a HYPOTHESIS label.

quoted_clause: "code, numerics, and non-Latin scripts routinely run 2-5x the naive word-count estimate"
observed: A specific quantitative range is asserted with no source, no tokenizer named, and no measurement. The upper end of the range is strongly tokenizer- and script-dependent, so the number is not portable - which is the point the surrounding bullet is making about the 4-chars-per-token heuristic.
evidence: No citation, measurement, or tokenizer is named in the chunk.
root_cause: An unsourced rule of thumb is stated with a numeric range, in a bullet whose whole point is that such rules must be measured.
correction: Either cite a tokenizer-specific measurement (e.g. 'for the canonical tokenizer, CJK text measured ~2.5x the word count') or soften to 'can run several times the naive word-count estimate'.
acceptance_test: The claim carries a source or is stated without a numeric range.

quoted_clause: "a decode cluster optimized for bandwidth (faster HBM, PagedAttention, continuous batching)"
observed: Mechanism mis-attribution. PagedAttention is a KV allocation and fragmentation strategy (memory capacity and allocator efficiency); continuous batching is a scheduling mechanism (utilization and queueing). Neither is a bandwidth optimization, and listing them under 'optimized for bandwidth' blurs exactly the mechanism taxonomy the book keeps sharp elsewhere (the review's own distinction between KV cache, PagedAttention, prefix caching, KV quantization and KV offloading).
evidence: The same chapter elsewhere treats PagedAttention and continuous batching as distinct mechanisms with distinct constraints; the list here groups them under a single constraint label without saying which constraint each relieves.
root_cause: The list was written as a shopping list rather than as a mapping from constraint to mechanism.
correction: Rewrite as 'a decode cluster optimized for sustained HBM bandwidth and KV residency (higher-bandwidth HBM; PagedAttention for KV allocation efficiency; continuous batching for decode-time utilization)'.
acceptance_test: Each named mechanism is attached to the constraint it actually relieves, and the list does not imply that PagedAttention or continuous batching increase bandwidth.

quoted_clause: "**-> Bound 5: the regulated-data requirement makes the local/server tier the primary path ...** [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)" | "**-> Bound 6: cost ceiling - within a self-host budget (Ch16).** [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)"
observed: Bounds 5 and 6 are outputs of the dialogue - a data-sensitivity constraint and a budget posture - not entries of the canonical scenario table. The uniform '(Ch 4, Table 4-2)' pointer implies they are tabulated canonical inputs, and the [canonical scenario] provenance label is applied to quantities the canonical table does not contain.
evidence: Bounds 1-4 map to Table 4-2 entries (traffic, token profile, SLO, quality set); Bounds 5 and 6 do not, and Bound 6's own text cites Ch 16 rather than Ch 4.
root_cause: A uniform citation and label were applied to all six bounds regardless of kind.
correction: Label Bounds 5 and 6 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (or [canonical scenario][DERIVED]) and cite Ch 13 / Ch 16 rather than Table 4-2.
acceptance_test: Each bound's label and pointer match the kind of quantity it is; no bound cites a table that does not contain it.

page_hint: Ch 24 §5 (Common Mistakes table) vs §4.2 and Table 24-1
quoted_clause: "10,000 probes may only explore 200 distinct injection patterns" | "Run at least 5 cycles; track the Red-team win rate across cycles."
observed: Two internal inconsistencies. (a) The mistake table's probe volume (10,000) appears nowhere else; §4.2 states the probe generator runs 1,000 probes per cycle and §3.1's candidate pattern space is 768. (b) The chapter prescribes at least five cycles, but its own worked example stops at three (Table 24-1, and §8's 'over three simulated cycles'), so the chapter's data violates the chapter's prescription without comment.
evidence: §4.2 item 1: 'runs 1,000 Red Team probes per cycle'; §3.1: 4 x 8 x 6 x 4 = 768; Table 24-1 has three cycle columns; §8: 'over three simulated cycles'.
root_cause: The mistake table was written against a different scenario scale than the one the chapter settled on.
correction: Align the numbers (e.g. '1,000 probes per cycle may explore only ~200 distinct patterns') and either extend the worked example to five cycles or state explicitly that the three-cycle table is a truncated illustration.
acceptance_test: Probe counts and cycle counts are consistent across §3, §4.2, §5, §8 and Table 24-1, and the worked example satisfies the chapter's own minimum-cycle rule or explains why not.

quoted_clause: "**Poisoned-hit rate** | DERIVED | Fraction of retrievals that return at least one poisoned chunk | < 0.3% (0.003 per query)"
observed: The target sits below the chapter's own null-model baseline, which is never noted. With 50 poisoned chunks in a 48,000-chunk corpus and k = 5, the uniform-retrieval model already predicts ~0.52% of retrievals containing at least one poisoned chunk - above the 0.3% target. A reader trying to hit the target from the chapter's own numbers will find it unreachable and will not know why.
evidence: 5 x 50/48,000 = 0.00521 = 0.52%; target 0.003 = 0.3%. Table 24-1 Cycle 1 (0.006) sits just above the null model, consistent with this.
root_cause: The target was chosen as a round number without reference to the baseline the chapter computes two sections earlier.
correction: Add one sentence to §4.1: 'note that the uniform-retrieval null model of §3.2 already predicts ~0.52% at 50 poisoned chunks, so a <0.3% target implicitly requires a larger corpus, fewer poisoned chunks, or a retrieval distribution less exposed than uniform.'
acceptance_test: The target is stated relative to the null-model baseline, and a reader can tell what must change to reach it.

quoted_clause: "For this workload both precisions clear the quality bar on the held-out Q&A set, with no exact-match change between them, so the deciding factors are range robustness and consistency - not capacity." | "A100 (and the 8xH100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores."
observed: Two wording defects in the same ADR. (a) The quality result is asserted in the indicative before its caveat ('we did not run this comparison on real hardware in this handbook; it is an assumed outcome'), inverting the claim-strength order the chapter is otherwise careful about - and the ADR's Status is 'Accepted'. (b) 'A100 (and the 8xH100 host)' conflates a GPU model with a server; an 8xH100 host does not 'natively support' anything on its Tensor Cores - the eight H100s do.
evidence: The same paragraph carries the caveat immediately after the assertion; the ADR's Status field reads 'Accepted'.
root_cause: Drafting order (assertion first, caveat appended) and a loose device/server noun phrase.
correction: Write 'H100 (and A100) Tensor Cores support BF16 and TF32 natively', and move the caveat ahead of the assertion: 'we have not run this comparison on real hardware; the worked ADR assumes no exact-match difference [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]'.
acceptance_test: No unmeasured result is stated in the indicative before its evidence label, and every device named in the ADR is a device that has the property claimed.

quoted_clause: "plus ~30 GB activations at the peak for this worked example (K+V alone: 2 x 80 layers x 9.2K x 8,192 x 2 B ~= 24 GB, plus hidden/MLP working tensors ~= 30 GB total)"
observed: 'Total' attaches to the wrong noun. As written, the hidden/MLP working tensors are ~30 GB, which would make the activations ~54 GB and the footprint ~194 GB - not the ~170 GB the next sentence states. The intended reading (24 GB K/V plus ~6 GB working tensors = ~30 GB) is recoverable only from the following sentence.
root_cause: Ambiguous attachment of 'total' inside a parenthetical that mixes a component and a sum.
correction: Write 'plus ~6 GB of hidden/MLP working tensors ~= 30 GB of activations in total'.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical and the stated 170 GB total agree without needing the next sentence to disambiguate.

quoted_clause: §8: "prompts of ~1,200 tokens of internal documents plus ~8K retrieved context" | §3 Step 1: "the prompt consists of ~1,200 tokens of query text plus ~8,000 tokens of retrieved RAG context"
observed: The same 1,200-token component is 'query text' in §3 and 'internal documents' in §8. These are different content and would tokenize differently, so the canonical prompt composition is described two ways within one chapter.
evidence: The two quoted clauses.
root_cause: The mini-case re-described the canonical prompt from memory rather than reusing the canonical definition.
correction: Use one description in both places, and if the mini-case is meant to vary the workload, say so explicitly and state which component changed.
acceptance_test: The canonical prompt composition is described identically wherever it appears in the book.

quoted_clause: "At 10 rps average, the system must sustain ~92,000 input tokens/s in prefill and ~3,000 output tokens/s in decode. At 40 rps peak, those numbers jump to ~368,000 and ~12,000 respectively."
observed: The mini-case reproduces the four token-rate numbers from Step 3 and Table 22-1 verbatim, and then the 1.29 PFLOP / 140 GB / 5.6 TB/s triple from §6, without adding a derivation or a decision. This is redundant repetition (class C) rather than reinforcement: the mini-case's stated job is to make a decision (homogeneous cluster vs separate prefill/decode pools) and it does not work any quantity toward that decision.
evidence: §3 Step 3, Table 22-1, §6 and §8 all carry the same numbers.
root_cause: The mini-case was written as a summary of the chapter rather than as a decision exercise.
correction: Compress the mini-case to the decision it makes and cite Table 22-1 for the numbers, or add a step the mini-case must actually work - e.g. sizing the burst buffer, or choosing the KV precision - so that the repetition advances the argument.
acceptance_test: The mini-case contains at least one quantity or decision not already derived in §3-§6, and the numbers it repeats are referenced rather than restated.

page_hint: Ch 22 §6 and Ch 25 §6 (the two 'DECISION STATE' callouts)
quoted_clause: "**DECISION STATE - CANDIDATE SCREENED; NOT COMMITTABLE - regional availability, failover, SLO-goodput and matched-scope costs pending.**" (appears in both chapters)
observed: The same callout with the same four pending items appears twice within four pages of text, differing only in the framing sentences around it. This is redundant repetition (class C) rather than reinforcement, and it sits immediately before two near-duplicate renderings of ADR 0015.
evidence: Ch 22 §6 and Ch 25 §6 both carry the callout and both carry ADR 0015 (the Ch 22 version explicitly says the full matrix is in Ch 25 §6).
root_cause: The callout was authored once and pasted into the second location.
correction: Keep the full callout in Ch 25, where the ADR record lives, and reduce the Ch 22 occurrence to a one-line pointer ('see ADR 0015, Ch 25 §6').
acceptance_test: The callout appears once in full; the second occurrence is a pointer, and the two ADR 0015 renderings are explicitly labelled as compact and full.

page_hint: Ch 22 Table 22-1 (KV row) vs Ch 24 §3.3 and Ch 25 §8
quoted_clause: Ch 22: "at 8-bit KV the same 9.2K context falls to ~12.06 GB under raw tensor byte-halving (2.62->1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of FP16)" | Ch 25: "Render the KV cache in FP8 for the long-context decode path" / "FP8 KV cuts KV residency to ~50% of the FP16 figure"
observed: The same one-byte-per-element KV format is called '8-bit KV' in Ch 22 and Ch 24 and 'FP8 KV' in Ch 25 (whose ADR title is 'FP16 vs FP8'). FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) and INT8 are different numerics with the same byte width, and the book never says which it means, so a reader cannot tell whether the precision claim in ADR 0017 is about a floating-point format or an integer one.
evidence: The quoted clauses; Ch 25 §8's ADR title 'ADR 0017 - KV Cache Precision: FP16 vs FP8'.
root_cause: Two names for one format were introduced in different chapters and never reconciled.
correction: Pick one term (recommend 'FP8 KV (E4M3)' for the format) and use it everywhere; where '8-bit' is used, define it once as the byte-width shorthand for the same format.
acceptance_test: A search for '8-bit KV' and 'FP8 KV' returns one format under one name, and the specific format (E4M3 vs INT8) is stated once and used consistently.

quoted_clause: "(see §3 for the deduplication rule)"
observed: The pointer is self-referential: the deduplication rule is stated in the same subsection (§3.1), immediately after the clause. The reference resolves to the enclosing section rather than to the rule.
evidence: The rule ('within NLE <= 0.25 of an existing class they are treated as equivalent') appears in the same paragraph.
root_cause: The rule was moved into §3.1 from a later subsection without updating the pointer.
correction: Change to '(see §3.1)' or drop the parenthetical, since the rule is in the same sentence.
acceptance_test: The pointer resolves to the subsection that contains the rule.

quoted_clause: "a two-week pilot on 5% of tickets to confirm the referral quality before full rollout" | "an arrival-rate buffer"
observed: Two wording defects. 'Referral quality' is not a property of a ticket-answering assistant (presumably 'resolution quality' or 'answer quality'). 'Arrival-rate buffer' is not a standard term for the mechanism described - arrivals buffered and drained at the sustainable rate - and the chapter's own §4.1 uses precise denominators for every other quantity.
evidence: The quoted clauses.
root_cause: Draft wording carried into a chapter whose standard is otherwise high.
correction: Use 'resolution quality' and 'a burst queue (arrivals buffered and drained at the sustainable rate)'.
acceptance_test: The terms used are either the book's own defined terms or standard terms, and the pilot's success metric names what is being measured.

quoted_clause: "decode lands in the bandwidth-bound regime at low batch (Ch6), prefill in the compute-bound regime at long prompt (Ch8)" | "the six bounds it extracts are exactly the inputs Ch1-17 consume" | "(Ch2-16 derive the constraints)"
observed: Three forms of the same construct appear in three consecutive chapters: 'Ch6', 'Ch1-17', 'Ch2-16', alongside 'Ch 4', 'Ch 7', 'Chapter 8' and 'Ch 16 §16.3'. In a book whose cross-references are its navigation system, and whose chapters are numbered with a hyphenated range in at least one place, this is a consistency defect that also makes range references ('Ch1-17') ambiguous with the book's own hyphenated identifiers (ADR 0015, Ch 16 §16.3).
evidence: The quoted clauses.
root_cause: No house style for chapter references was applied across the manuscript.
correction: Adopt one form per context - 'Ch 6' in parentheticals, 'Chapter 8' in prose, 'Ch 1-17' written as 'Ch 1-17' with an en dash - and sweep the source.
acceptance_test: A search of the source shows one chapter-reference form per context, and no range reference can be confused with an ADR or section identifier.
